The authors examine how this hybrid approach was developed and operationalized, while identifying significant challenges regarding implementation capability, alignment with democratic principles, and the regulation's capacity to accommodate rapid technological evolution.

papers.note: Addresses the hard case of systems that keep learning after deployment, which fixed trial designs cannot cover.
papers.title: Rethinking clinical trials for medical AI with dynamic deployments of adaptive systems
papers.explain_beginner: Medical AI systems, especially those using large language models, keep learning and improving after they're released to hospitals. Traditional clinical trials test a frozen system once, then it goes live unchanged. This paper proposes a better approach where AI systems continue learning in real hospitals under careful monitoring. Doctors can track whether the system stays safe and effective as it adapts, catching problems quickly rather than discovering them months later.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying medical AI can now move beyond choosing between slow traditional approval or risky unmonitored deployment. Dynamic deployment enables companies to launch learning systems while maintaining regulatory compliance through continuous monitoring. This reduces time-to-market for evolving medical AI, supports faster improvement cycles, and provides documented evidence of safety and effectiveness in actual clinical use, ultimately enabling more sophisticated medical AI applications to reach patients sooner.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper presents dynamic deployment as a clinical trial framework designed for continuously-learning AI systems in medical settings. Unlike conventional trials that validate static models pre-deployment, this approach enables large language model-based medical AI to learn from real clinical interactions and new data post-deployment while maintaining concurrent monitoring and validation. The framework permits complex adaptive systems to operate in clinical environments with real-time safety oversight and performance assessment throughout their operational lifecycle.

papers.note: Points out that deep-learning systems cannot be audited against a specification the way aircraft can, then argues the expert-agency model still applies, with licensing, disclosure and rapid intervention.
papers.title: When code is not law: rethinking regulation for artificial intelligence

papers.note: Assesses United States governance strategy specifically, including the legal risks attaching to generated content, and proposes where a dedicated regulator would help.
papers.title: Balancing Innovation and Regulation in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
papers.explain_beginner: New AI tools like ChatGPT are spreading rapidly through society, creating both exciting possibilities and serious concerns. This paper examines the legal problems these tools create, particularly around content they generate, and explores how governments should regulate them. The authors studied US law and governance approaches, then recommend creating a dedicated regulator and stronger international coordination to protect people while still allowing innovation to continue.
papers.explain_business: Generative AI adoption is accelerating, but legal uncertainty creates business risk. This research identifies critical gaps in current US regulation of AI-generated content and recommends establishing dedicated oversight. For executives, this signals that regulatory clarity is coming, making early compliance investment prudent. The study supports the case for industry participation in developing new regulatory frameworks and suggests monitoring international coordination efforts that will shape operational requirements.
papers.explain_practitioner: This study conducted literature review, legal doctrinal analysis, and case study examination of generative AI governance in the United States. The authors analyzed current legal frameworks and their limitations, then synthesized research on technological and ethical implications. Key finding: existing US governance strategies have significant gaps. The paper proposes establishing a dedicated regulatory body combined with harmonized international collaboration and proactive legislation to address legal risks from AI-generated content while preserving innovation capacity.

papers.note: A working health system governance structure with committees, guiding principles and a value stream, not just principles.
papers.title: Governance of Clinical AI applications to facilitate safe and equitable deployment in a large health system

papers.note: Turns the seven trustworthiness requirements into a certification oriented assurance process with residual risk quantification.
papers.title: Trustworthiness Assurance Assessment for High-Risk AI-Based Systems

papers.note: Written as a primer for clinicians rather than engineers, and explicit that hallucination and poor generalisation remain blockers to adoption.
papers.title: Large language models in oncology: a review
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers reviewed how artificial intelligence systems that understand and generate human language could help cancer doctors and patients. These systems show promise for helping doctors make decisions, pulling important information from medical records, and supporting patients emotionally. However, major challenges exist before hospitals can safely use them, including the systems sometimes inventing false information and struggling to work reliably across different situations. The authors suggest combining these systems with other technologies to make them more trustworthy and useful in cancer care.
papers.explain_business: This review indicates that while language AI systems could meaningfully support cancer care operations by automating administrative tasks and enhancing clinical workflows, significant technical and safety barriers prevent immediate deployment. Organizations considering adoption should prioritize resolving hallucination and reliability issues before implementation. The recommended approach involves combining language AI with other technologies and implementing rigorous evaluation processes. This positions language AI as a medium-term investment requiring careful validation rather than an immediate operational solution, with success depending on systematic technical improvements and clear governance frameworks.
papers.explain_practitioner: This narrative review surveys large language model applications across three oncology domains: clinician support through decision assistance and automated clinical data extraction, patient-facing tools for information access and psychosocial support, and translational research acceleration. The authors identify critical limitations including hallucination generation, generalization failures, ethical concerns, and integration challenges that currently impede clinical deployment. They recommend embedding LLMs within composite AI architectures to enhance reliability and clinical utility. The review emphasizes that robust evaluation frameworks are necessary before adoption, positioning LLMs as augmentative rather than replacement technologies for oncology practice.

papers.note: Recent PRISMA review of AI in clinical risk management, covering incident reporting, falls and medication error.
papers.title: Artificial intelligence in healthcare: transforming patient safety with intelligent systems: A systematic review
papers.explain_beginner: Hospitals face serious problems from medical errors that harm patients and erode trust in healthcare. This research review examined how artificial intelligence could help prevent these mistakes. Scientists found that AI tools can successfully spot dangerous situations, predict medication errors, and identify patients at risk of falling or developing pressure wounds. However, putting these systems into actual hospitals remains difficult due to organizational and technical challenges that need solving before widespread adoption.
papers.explain_business: Healthcare organizations exploring patient safety investments should recognize AI's validated capability in error prevention and incident detection. Practical applications exist for medication safety, fall prevention, and wound management. However, executives must account for significant implementation costs related to organizational change, staff training, and system integration challenges. Success requires partnerships with vendors willing to address regulatory standards and clinical workflow requirements. This technology represents a strategic opportunity, but requires phased implementation with clear metrics rather than immediate enterprise-wide deployment.
papers.explain_practitioner: This PRISMA-compliant systematic review evaluated AI applications in clinical risk management across incident reporting, falls prevention, and medication safety. Researchers screened studies using Rayyan across multiple databases. Machine learning and natural language processing demonstrated effectiveness in adverse event detection, error prediction, risk stratification, and automated incident classification. Key findings revealed improved reporting accuracy and high-risk identification, though socio-technical barriers, implementation obstacles, and standardization gaps limit clinical integration. The authors recommend continued development with iterative refinement and regulatory alignment before scaling these systems in healthcare environments.

papers.note: Models AI audit on financial audit practice and works the criteria through NYC Local Law 144 bias audits.
papers.title: A Framework for Assurance Audits of Algorithmic Systems
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency

papers.note: Focuses on enforcement capacity rather than drafting, on the argument that regulation without enforcement is nothing, and recommends a model for coordinating supranational and national bodies.
papers.title: A Robust Governance for the AI Act: AI Office, AI Board, Scientific Panel, and National Authorities
papers.explain_beginner: The European Union created new rules for artificial intelligence, but having rules means nothing if nobody enforces them. This paper examines who is responsible for making sure companies follow these AI rules and proposes a better system for coordination. The authors explain how different European institutions and national governments should work together to monitor AI companies and ensure everyone follows the same standards fairly.
papers.explain_business: The AI Act requires robust enforcement to be effective, and this paper clarifies the governance structure organizations must navigate. Companies need to understand which European bodies and national authorities will oversee compliance, as implementation varies across member states. The proposed coordination model indicates businesses should expect consistent regulatory standards, but compliance strategies must account for both EU-level oversight and national authority involvement in enforcement actions.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors analyzed the enforcement mechanisms of the EU's Artificial Intelligence Act across institutional bodies including the European Commission, the newly created AI Office, and national authorities. They mapped roles and responsibilities at both supranational and national levels, examining how regulatory requirements shape institutional capacity and structure. The paper proposes a coordinated governance model designed to achieve consistent implementation and enforcement of the AIA across member states, addressing the administrative and operational requirements necessary for effective regulation execution.

papers.note: Combines state space models with mixture of experts and open sources the weights, a live alternative to transformer scaling.
papers.title: BlackMamba: Mixture of Experts for State-Space Models

papers.note: Categorises 283 benchmarks into general, domain specific and target specific, a map for choosing evidence.
papers.title: A Survey on Large Language Model Benchmarks

papers.note: Defines clinical hazards, constrains the action space, and retrains for safety without losing performance, a replicable method.
papers.title: Assuring the safety of AI-based clinical decision support systems: a case study of the AI Clinician for sepsis treatment
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested an AI system designed to recommend treatments for sepsis, a life-threatening infection. They identified four dangerous medical situations the AI should avoid, then checked whether the AI made safer recommendations than human doctors. The AI performed better in most cases. The team then adjusted how the AI learns to prioritize safety, and confirmed the improved version made safer choices without becoming less effective overall. This work shows how to carefully verify AI medical tools are trustworthy before using them in hospitals.
papers.explain_business: This research demonstrates a practical framework for safely deploying AI in clinical settings before regulatory approval. By systematically identifying medical risks and retraining the system to avoid them, the company can build confidence with hospitals and regulators. The approach preserves the AI's effectiveness while eliminating dangerous recommendations, reducing liability and approval timelines. This methodology is reproducible across different AI applications and clinical domains, providing a competitive advantage in developing trustworthy medical AI products that regulators will more readily approve for real-world deployment.
papers.explain_practitioner: We conducted safety assurance on an AI Clinician reinforcement learning system for sepsis management. We defined four clinical hazards based on expert consensus and literature review, then identified unsafe scenarios to constrain the agent's action space. Testing against MIMIC-III data showed the AI recommended fewer hazardous decisions than clinicians in three of four scenarios. We modified the reward function to enforce safety constraints and retrained the model. The resulting agent demonstrated improved safety while maintaining predictive performance, establishing a replicable methodology for systematic safety assurance of autonomous clinical decision support systems.

papers.note: Covers Model Context Protocol tool poisoning and RAG poisoning, and maps defences to OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025.
papers.title: Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models and AI Agent Systems: A Comprehensive Review of Vulnerabilities, Attack Vectors, and Defense Mechanisms
papers.explain_beginner: This paper examines a major security problem with AI language models: attackers can trick them into ignoring their instructions and misbehaving. As these AI systems become more integrated into real applications, new attack methods have emerged, especially through connected tools and external data sources. The researchers found that attackers can manipulate AI responses with surprising ease, and they propose a multi-layered defense strategy to protect against these threats.
papers.explain_business: Prompt injection attacks pose substantial risk to deployed AI systems, with documented severe incidents like remote code execution vulnerabilities and credential theft. Minimal attack effort achieves high success rates, particularly when data sources are involved. Organizations implementing AI agents must adopt comprehensive, layered security approaches aligned with OWASP standards rather than relying on single defenses. This represents an ongoing architectural challenge requiring continuous monitoring and evolving protection strategies as threat vectors expand.
papers.explain_practitioner: This comprehensive review analyzes prompt injection vulnerabilities in LLMs and agent systems from 2023-2025, examining 45 sources and real exploits. It categorizes attack vectors including direct jailbreaking, indirect injection via external content, tool poisoning through MCP, and RAG poisoning demonstrating 90% manipulation success with five documents. Critical incidents documented include CVE-2025-53773 (CVSS 9.6) and credential leakage. The authors propose PALADIN, a five-layer defense framework, and map mitigations to OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, identifying fundamental limitations requiring architectural rather than tactical solutions.

papers.note: Maps which underlying capabilities matter in which domain, and proposes evaluation tailored to the domain rather than to a general benchmark.
papers.title: Fundamental Capabilities and Applications of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models work well in many fields, but we don't fully understand which of their core strengths matter most for different jobs. This survey maps out the fundamental abilities these models possess and shows how different domains rely on different combinations of these abilities. Rather than using one-size-fits-all tests, the researchers suggest evaluating models based on the specific skills each field actually needs, making it easier to choose the right model for the job.
papers.explain_business: When deploying language models in production, selecting the right model requires understanding which capabilities matter for your specific application. This research provides a practical framework to identify which model strengths align with your domain's actual needs, whether healthcare, legal services, or financial analysis. Rather than relying on generic performance scores, companies can now evaluate models against the precise capabilities their business processes require, reducing deployment risk and improving real-world outcomes.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey systematically documents LLM fundamental capabilities, their formation mechanisms, and interconnections, then analyzes their application across nine domains including medicine, law, finance, and software engineering. The authors establish explicit mappings between specific capabilities and domain-specific requirements, revealing that standard benchmarks often misalign with real-world performance needs. The key contribution is domain-tailored evaluation frameworks that prioritize assessing capabilities relevant to each application's unique demands rather than universal performance metrics.

papers.note: Uses product quality models to interpret high risk requirements across a multi party automotive supply chain.
papers.title: Navigating the EU AI Act: A Methodological Approach to Compliance for Safety-critical Products

papers.note: Analyses twelve African countries and finds usable governance capability already sitting in banking model management and electronic transactions law, rather than assuming a blank slate.
papers.title: Responsible artificial intelligence in Africa: towards policy learning

papers.note: Finds performance on commonsense tasks varies by culture and by the language the question is asked in, which is a concrete measurement of a bias usually discussed abstractly.
papers.title: Understanding the Capabilities and Limitations of Large Language Models for Cultural Commonsense
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested whether large language models, like chatbots, understand common sense the same way across different cultures. They found these systems perform better on some cultural tasks than others, and surprisingly, they work differently depending on what language you ask the question in. This matters because it shows AI systems have hidden biases that favor certain cultures, which could lead to unfair or unhelpful responses for people from underrepresented groups.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying language models must recognize that these systems perform inconsistently across different cultural contexts and languages. This has direct implications for global applications, customer service, and content moderation. Companies should conduct culture and language specific testing before deployment, expect variable quality in different markets, and plan localization strategies rather than assuming one model works equally well everywhere.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study evaluated large language models on cultural commonsense reasoning tasks across multiple cultures and languages. Performance varied significantly based on both the cultural context of the task and the language used for questioning. This demonstrates that model capabilities are not uniform across cultural domains and that language choice influences task performance, indicating that cultural representation in training data and evaluation methodologies requires careful consideration.

papers.note: Nurses performed worse when the AI was misleading, so model accuracy alone does not make the joint system safe.
papers.title: Empirically derived evaluation requirements for responsible deployments of AI in safety-critical settings
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested whether artificial intelligence could help nurses spot medical emergencies faster. They found that while AI accuracy matters, it is not enough on its own. When the AI gave wrong explanations, nurses made worse decisions, even if the AI's answers were correct. The study shows that deploying AI in hospitals requires testing how humans and AI work together, not just checking if the AI works well by itself.
papers.explain_business: Organizations considering AI deployment in safety-critical environments like healthcare need assessment protocols beyond vendor accuracy claims. This research demonstrates that poor AI explanations actively harm decision quality despite correct recommendations, creating liability risks. Decision makers should require vendors to demonstrate human-AI team performance on diverse test cases, including scenarios where the AI performs poorly, before deployment approval or purchase decisions.
papers.explain_practitioner: This empirical study evaluated three augmentative AI systems for clinical decision support with 450 nursing students and 12 licensed nurses assessing 10 patient cases. Results demonstrated that nurse performance improved with accurate AI but degraded significantly when receiving misleading explanations, regardless of algorithmic correctness. The authors propose two evaluation requirements for safety-critical AI deployment: measure joint human-AI system performance empirically rather than AI performance alone, and test across cases generating varied AI quality levels to identify failure modes.

papers.note: Bypasses all eight tested defences at over 50 percent success, so any vendor injection defence claim needs adaptive testing.
papers.title: Adaptive Attacks Break Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Agents
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers tested eight different security protections designed to stop a specific type of attack on AI assistants that use external tools and information. They found that with clever, adaptive attacks, they could break through every single protection more than half the time. This matters because companies relying on these defenses might think their systems are safer than they actually are, potentially exposing users to harmful manipulation.
papers.explain_business: Current marketed defenses against prompt injection attacks are not as effective as claimed when tested against sophisticated attackers. Any vendor claiming protection against this threat should undergo rigorous adaptive testing to validate their claims. Organizations deploying LLM agents with external tool access should recognize that existing defenses have significant gaps and require additional safeguards or architectural changes before relying on them for security-critical applications.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study evaluated eight defense mechanisms against indirect prompt injection attacks targeting LLM agents with tool integration. Using adaptive attacks tailored to each defense's specific approach, researchers achieved over 50 percent bypass rates across all tested defenses. The key finding is that static defense evaluations are insufficient; adaptive attack testing that evolves based on defense characteristics is necessary to properly assess robustness and identify fundamental vulnerabilities in protection mechanisms.

papers.note: A dissent from the consensus: argues risk classification underweights circular effects, the difficulty of measuring risk at all, and geopolitical power imbalance.
papers.title: Limitations of risk-based artificial intelligence regulation: a structuration theory approach
papers.explain_beginner: Most countries now regulate AI by sorting systems into risk categories, with stricter rules for high-risk applications. This paper argues that approach has blind spots. It misses how AI systems create ripple effects across society, struggles to measure risk accurately, and ignores that powerful nations shape global AI rules. The authors suggest viewing AI as an active force that reshapes society itself, rather than just a tool to control, would lead to better regulation.
papers.explain_business: Risk-based AI regulation, while providing clear compliance categories, may create false confidence and regulatory arbitrage opportunities. Organizations should anticipate that current frameworks will evolve as policymakers recognize measurement limitations and unintended consequences of deployment. Companies should prepare for more sophisticated, adaptive regulatory approaches that treat AI as a structural force, not merely a controllable tool. This suggests investing in broader stakeholder engagement and impact monitoring beyond checklist compliance.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study examines risk-based AI regulation frameworks, particularly the EU AI Act, and identifies structural gaps. The analysis reveals that categorical risk assessment fails to capture feedback loops between AI deployment and social structures, measurement uncertainty undermines classification reliability, and geopolitical asymmetries influence regulatory design. The authors propose structuration theory as an analytical framework, positioning AI systems as active agents that co-constitute social structures, offering a more comprehensive lens for regulatory development that acknowledges AI's recursive influence on institutional and social arrangements.

papers.note: Governance as code with signed evidence artifacts and clause level traceability across EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001.
papers.title: From Policy to Pipeline: A Governance Framework for AI Development and Operations Pipelines
papers.explain_beginner: This paper presents a new system for ensuring artificial intelligence applications follow important rules and laws. Rather than checking compliance after a system is built, this approach weaves rules directly into the development process itself. The system automatically collects evidence at each stage of building and running AI, creates tamper-proof records, and proves that regulations like the EU AI Act are being followed. Using a hospital early-warning system as an example, the authors show this makes AI development more transparent, trustworthy, and accountable.
papers.explain_business: This framework reduces compliance risk by embedding regulatory requirements directly into development pipelines rather than relying on manual, retrospective auditing. Organizations gain automatically generated audit evidence and can demonstrate accountability across multiple regulations simultaneously. The approach accelerates time-to-market by eliminating manual compliance documentation work while increasing confidence in high-risk deployments. For regulated industries like healthcare and finance, this provides deterministic proof of compliance and significantly reduces legal exposure when regulations are contested or audited.
papers.explain_practitioner: GEAP implements governance as executable code integrated into ML pipelines across five control gates: Data, Training, Validation, Release, and Operations. Each gate generates signed, content-addressed artifacts stored in an Evidence Backbone. The framework automatically maps these artifacts to specific regulatory clauses across EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and ISO/IEC 42001 through deterministic traceability, eliminating manual documentation. Governance metrics quantify adequacy, completeness, stability, and evidence quality. A sepsis detection system case study validates that GEAP enforces promotion policies, detects violations, and produces audit-ready compliance bundles automatically.

papers.note: A production grade system combining linear sequence modeling with sparse activation, relevant to inference cost planning.
papers.title: Linear-MoE: Linear Sequence Modeling Meets Mixture-of-Experts

papers.note: Digital ageism is rarely covered elsewhere, and this mitigates it without touching model parameters.
papers.title: Mitigating Age-Related Bias in Large Language Models: Strategies for Responsible Artificial Intelligence Development
papers.explain_beginner: This research tackles a hidden problem: artificial intelligence systems sometimes treat older people unfairly or give them worse results than younger people. The scientists created a method called FairLLM that helps AI systems recognize and fix these age-related mistakes without rebuilding the system from scratch. The solution uses techniques inspired by human empathy, teamwork between multiple AI systems, and human oversight to make the AI more aware of its biases and generate fairer responses for people of all ages.
papers.explain_business: Age bias in AI systems creates legal, reputational, and fairness risks for organizations deploying language models in customer-facing applications. This work demonstrates a practical framework that improves fairness outcomes without expensive model retraining or replacement. For executives, the parameter-free approach means faster implementation and lower technical barriers to adoption. The cooperative bias detection model suggests scalability across different deployment scenarios. Organizations can reduce exposure to digital discrimination claims while improving user experience across demographic groups, particularly benefiting underserved older populations.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper presents a two-stage bias mitigation framework addressing age-related discrimination in LLMs through parameter-free mechanisms. The approach employs two operational modes: autonomous self-assessment where models identify and correct their own age biases, and cooperative modes leveraging multi-model consensus through debate. A key innovation is the empathetic perspective exchange strategy, which reframes context to generate age-appropriate responses. Evaluation on multiple datasets shows FairLLM substantially reduces age bias metrics compared to baseline methods, utilizing reinforcement learning and human-in-the-loop validation throughout the pipeline.

papers.note: Comparative analysis of where AI Act duties layer on top of GDPR rather than replacing them.
papers.title: Reflections on the data protection compliance of AI systems under the EU AI Act
papers.explain_beginner: The European Union created a new law specifically for artificial intelligence systems called the AI Act. This paper examines how this new law works alongside an existing privacy law called GDPR. The researchers found that the AI Act adds extra rules on top of GDPR rather than replacing it, especially for higher-risk AI systems. The law tries to address problems like biased decisions and secret AI decision-making by requiring companies to be more transparent and careful. While the AI Act generally supports the same fairness goals as GDPR, it creates more paperwork and compliance tasks for AI developers.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying AI systems in Europe must now comply with two layered regulatory frameworks rather than relying on GDPR alone. The AI Act imposes additional compliance costs through new risk assessment, documentation, and oversight requirements, particularly for higher-risk applications. This means companies cannot simply meet GDPR standards and assume legal compliance. Decision-makers should budget for enhanced governance infrastructure and legal expertise to navigate both regulations simultaneously. The stricter requirements create barriers to rapid deployment but establish clearer standards for trustworthy AI, potentially offering competitive advantages for early-compliance leaders and reducing long-term regulatory risk.
papers.explain_practitioner: This comparative legal analysis evaluates how the AI Act's risk-based regulatory framework interacts with GDPR requirements for AI system developers. The study examined whether the new legislation clarifies compliance obligations or adds regulatory overlap. Findings indicate the AI Act functions as a complementary, stricter layer addressing gaps in GDPR, particularly regarding algorithmic transparency, bias mitigation, and automated decision-making. Implementation requires enhanced risk assessment procedures, mandatory human oversight mechanisms, and strengthened data governance practices. The analysis reveals that joint interpretation of both regulations is necessary for coherent application, though this increases documentation and procedural complexity for organizations developing high-risk AI systems.

papers.note: Proposes a benchmark lifecycle covering design, validation, monitoring and retirement, an audit ready framing.
papers.title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Survey of the Science of Evaluation, Benchmarking, and Methodologies for Large Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: This paper identifies a major problem in AI: popular test scores for large language models do not actually measure what we think they measure. Although these AI systems score well on standard tests, they often fail in real situations by making mistakes or producing harmful content. The researchers argue we need better evaluation methods that assess genuine capabilities rather than pursuing high scores on leaderboards. They propose a structured lifecycle for creating, checking, and retiring evaluation tools to make progress measurement more trustworthy.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying large language models face a critical risk: public benchmark scores do not predict real-world performance. This paper demonstrates why relying solely on leaderboard rankings to select models is unreliable and why purchased or built systems may underperform expectations. The proposed Benchmark Lifecycle framework provides a structured methodology for enterprises to properly evaluate AI systems before deployment, reducing failure risk. This guidance helps organizations establish evaluation as a scientific process rather than a competitive metric, ensuring confident decision-making for AI investments.
papers.explain_practitioner: The survey examines the disconnect between benchmark performance and practical LLM capabilities, attributing it to static evaluation paradigms. The authors present a taxonomy covering five evaluation approaches: static benchmarks, dynamic adaptive evaluation, interactive agentic evaluation, human-in-the-loop methods, and model-based evaluation. They analyze key pathologies including data contamination and leaderboard gaming. The central contribution is the Benchmark Lifecycle framework, which systematizes evaluation instrument development through design, validation, deployment monitoring, and retirement phases to enable rigorous measurement aligned with actual model behavior.

papers.note: Concludes high risk agentic systems with untraceable behavioural drift cannot currently meet AI Act essential requirements.
papers.title: AI Agents Under EU Law
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers examined how new AI systems that make decisions and take actions independently must follow European Union laws. These systems are being used in banks, hospitals, and other organizations, but they can behave unexpectedly in ways that are hard to trace. The study found that some of these systems cannot currently meet legal requirements because their behavior drifts in unpredictable ways. Companies deploying them must first map out everything the system can do and who it affects.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying autonomous AI agents across enterprise functions must recognize they face overlapping obligations under multiple EU regulations, not just the AI Act. The research identifies that systems with unpredictable behavioral changes cannot currently achieve legal compliance. Business leaders should prioritize building comprehensive inventories of what their agents can do, where data flows, which systems they connect to, and who they impact. This foundational compliance work is now essential before scaling agent deployments in high-risk domains like recruitment, clinical support, or infrastructure management.
papers.explain_practitioner: This paper systematically maps AI agent deployment against EU regulatory frameworks including the AI Act, GDPR, NIS2, and seven additional regimes, incorporating draft standards from CEN/CENELEC and the GPAI Code of Practice. The authors developed a nine-category taxonomy connecting agent actions to regulatory triggers and identified compliance gaps in cybersecurity, oversight, multi-party transparency, and behavioral drift detection. They propose a twelve-step architecture for compliance. Key finding: high-risk agents exhibiting untraceable runtime drift cannot satisfy current AI Act essential requirements without exhaustive documentation of external actions, data flows, system integrations, and affected stakeholders.

papers.note: Extends the NIST adversarial machine learning taxonomy across 88 studies and catalogues defence effectiveness by model.
papers.title: A Systematic Literature Review on LLM Defenses Against Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking: Expanding NIST Taxonomy
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models like ChatGPT can be tricked by carefully written prompts that make them leak secrets, perform unauthorized tasks, or give false information. Researchers reviewed 88 studies on ways to protect against these attacks and organized their findings using a framework from the US government agency NIST. The work identifies different defense strategies, measures how well each one works with different models, and creates a practical guide for developers building safer AI systems.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying large language models face significant security risks from prompt injection attacks that can cause data breaches or system misuse. This research catalogs proven defense strategies with measured effectiveness across different models, enabling technical teams to select appropriate protections based on their specific systems and threat profiles. The standardized framework and open-source solutions identified help companies implement defenses efficiently while reducing security vulnerabilities and potential liability from AI system compromise.
papers.explain_practitioner: This systematic review analyzed 88 peer-reviewed studies on prompt injection defenses and extended NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy with additional defense categories. The authors documented quantitative effectiveness metrics for mitigation strategies across specific LLMs and attack datasets, cataloguing which defenses are open-source and model-agnostic. By establishing standardized terminology and taxonomy grounded in NIST's framework, the work provides a structured foundation for comparing defense mechanisms and enables reproducible research for developing more robust LLM security solutions.

papers.note: Ranks which high risk requirements companies find hardest, with Article 10 data governance first and Article 15 second.
papers.title: AI Act high-risk AI compliance challenge and industry impact: A multiple case study

papers.note: Explains how to calibrate controls to risk severity, and treats NIS2 and DORA as risk multipliers on the same system.
papers.title: Risk, Reasonableness and Residual Harm under the EU AI Act: A Conceptual Framework for Proportional Ex-Ante Controls

papers.note: Prices fairness breaches against the AI Act fine tiers using 12.4 million real underwriting records, a rare quantified case.
papers.title: Algorithmic Bias Under the EU AI Act: Compliance Risk, Capital Strain, and Pricing Distortions in Life and Health Insurance Underwriting

papers.note: Addresses the common client case of using pretrained or off the shelf models, and ties actions to ISO 27090 and OWASP.
papers.title: Compliance Made Practical: Translating the EU AI Act into Implementable Security Actions
papers.journal: IEEE/ACM International Workshop on Responsible AI Engineering
papers.explain_beginner: New AI regulations in Europe require companies to make their AI systems secure, but it's unclear what concrete steps they should take. This paper explains how companies using existing AI models can follow these rules by connecting regulatory requirements to practical security actions. It bridges the gap between official guidelines and real-world implementation, helping organizations understand their responsibilities and what they must do to protect their systems.
papers.explain_business: Organizations deploying commercial or pretrained AI models now face regulatory compliance obligations under EU AI Act and emerging ISO 27090 standards, but lack clear implementation roadmaps. This work translates regulatory requirements into specific, achievable security actions your teams can execute. It enables informed decisions about risk mitigation investments, clarifies compliance responsibilities, and provides a framework for demonstrating due diligence to regulators and stakeholders.
papers.explain_practitioner: This work synthesizes the EU AI Act's security mandates with ISO/IEC standards and OWASP frameworks to create actionable implementation guidance. The paper maps regulatory requirements onto practical security strategies, specifically addressing the common scenario of deploying pretrained or commercial models. It provides concrete mitigation approaches tied to ISO 27090 and OWASP standards, clarifying responsibility allocation and sufficient compliance measures for practitioners building AI systems with existing components.

papers.note: Maps AI Act articles down to concrete verification activities by lifecycle stage, directly reusable as an audit programme.
papers.title: Assessing High-Risk AI Systems under the EU AI Act: From Legal Requirements to Technical Verification
papers.explain_beginner: The European Union's AI Act sets rules for high-risk artificial intelligence systems, but companies and regulators weren't sure how to actually check if AI systems followed these rules. This paper creates a practical guide that breaks down the legal requirements into specific, testable activities that can be checked at different stages of building and running AI systems. It helps everyone understand and verify compliance in the same way.
papers.explain_business: Companies deploying high-risk AI systems in Europe now have a clear, standardized methodology for demonstrating compliance with the AI Act. This framework reduces legal uncertainty, enables consistent audits across regions, and provides a reusable compliance roadmap that works regardless of AI technology type. Organizations can use this to streamline their compliance programs, reduce assessment costs, and demonstrate regulatory readiness to authorities and stakeholders.
papers.explain_practitioner: We systematically decomposed EU AI Act articles into operational sub-requirements grounded in established standards and practices. We then mapped these requirements to concrete verification activities characterized by verification type and lifecycle stage. The resulting framework translates high-level regulatory obligations into implementable, technology-agnostic assessment procedures across the full AI development cycle, reducing ambiguity in compliance interpretation and enabling consistent, auditable verification processes.

papers.note: Matches a dense Mamba needing 2.3x more active parameters, a concrete efficiency number for the state space line.
papers.title: Routing Mamba: Scaling State Space Models with Mixture-of-Experts Projection

papers.note: Side by side comparison of ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini on metrics, capabilities and limits, useful when a buyer asks which model to pick.
papers.title: CAPABILITIES AND LIMITATIONS OF LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS

papers.note: Separates the duties of each supply chain actor and explains when a deployer inherits full provider obligations.
papers.title: Obligations of importers, distributors and deployers of high-risk AI systems under the AI Act
papers.explain_beginner: The European Union's AI Act creates rules for different companies involved in selling and using high-risk artificial intelligence systems. This paper explains what each company must do. Importers and distributors mainly verify that products meet safety standards, while companies actually using the AI have separate responsibilities for managing risks during operation. Interestingly, if someone modifies an AI system, they may suddenly face the same strict rules as the original maker. Understanding these different roles matters because it helps everyone avoid penalties and reduces dangers from AI systems.
papers.explain_business: Organizations must understand their specific role in AI supply chains under EU regulations to avoid substantial fines. Importers face more demanding compliance verification than distributors, while companies deploying AI systems carry distinct accountability for managing risks during use. A key practical insight is that modifying purchased AI systems can create full provider-level compliance obligations. This means companies should audit whether their modifications trigger enhanced responsibilities. Clear identification of supply chain roles and potential obligation shifts is critical for compliance strategy, financial planning, and operational risk management across European markets.
papers.explain_practitioner: This work analyzes EU AI Act compliance obligations across the supply chain for high-risk systems. Importers perform primary verification of provider compliance while distributors have narrower verification duties. Deployers carry independent, non-subordinate obligations focused on operational risks rather than design compliance. The analysis identifies a critical scenario where modifications to AI systems trigger provider-equivalent obligations on actors who were not original deployers. This stems from AI susceptibility to purpose drift independent of original design intent. Clarifying these distinctions across importers, distributors, and deployers is essential for regulatory compliance and risk mitigation.

reading.body:
Chain-of-thought prompting, with 20,046 citations, is the single most cited result in this collection, and the data show why: it reframed reasoning as an inference-time technique rather than a training problem, which changed what every subsequent paper had to account for.

The 134 papers sort into a recognizable pattern. A capability gets demonstrated at scale, then a follow-on paper shows the demonstration was fragile. Chain-of-thought improves reasoning; GSM-Symbolic finds that changing only the numbers in a math problem degrades every model tested, and adding one irrelevant clause cuts performance by up to 65 percent. Med-PaLM passes USMLE-style questions; Hager et al. test the same class of models against 2,400 real intensive-care cases and find they diagnose worse than physicians and ignore treatment guidelines. Safety alignment ships; Andriushchenko et al. achieve 100 percent jailbreak success across major frontier models using simple adaptive search. The collection does not resolve these pairs. It records them.

The healthcare cluster is the densest by paper count, spanning five entries from 2019 through 2024, and it illustrates the pattern most sharply. The 2019 Kelly et al. paper on why clinical AI stalls between research and practice reads as a prediction; the 2024 Hager et al. paper in Nature Medicine reads as its confirmation. That gap is five years and many compute generations wide, and the data do not show it closing. What the data do not cover is the infrastructure side: nothing here addresses the compute cost, power draw, or facility requirements behind the models being evaluated, so readers wanting to connect clinical capability claims to the resource constraints that produce them will need to look elsewhere on this site.

The gap between benchmark performance and real-world capability is not incidental; it reflects a fundamental asymmetry in what models optimize for. Chain-of-thought prompting reveals this directly. Models that pass math exams by reasoning step-by-step fail when numbers change or irrelevant clauses appear, because they have learned to pattern-match problem structure rather than execute generalizable logic. The same asymmetry appears in medicine: models that clear USMLE licensing questions ignore treatment protocols and diagnose worse than physicians on actual patient cases. These are not edge cases or scaling artifacts. They are the expected behavior of systems trained to maximize likelihood on static benchmarks rather than robustness to distribution shift. The 134 papers in this collection do not attempt to reconcile capability and fragility; instead, they document both sides of the gap in parallel, creating a record of what capability claims do not yet account for.

The healthcare papers form a causal sequence that the field has not resolved. Kelly et al. in 2019 identified the barriers preventing clinical AI deployment: validation rigor, meaningful metrics, regulatory clarity, and post-hoc accountability. Five years later, Hager et al. demonstrate that those barriers remain active. Models passing medical exams still fail on real cases, still ignore guidelines, still misprocess data. The intervening papers—Med-PaLM on USMLE performance, the multimodal survey showing hallucination as an unresolved problem, the framework paper on bias in clinical settings—show researchers aware of these gaps but unable to close them. The data suggest the obstacle is not understanding what needs to be fixed but achieving it at scale while maintaining the capabilities that made the models valuable in the first place.

Safety and reasoning papers show a parallel pattern. After Wei et al. established that reasoning emerges through prompting, subsequent papers systematically identified the boundaries of that emergence: models handle single deduction steps but fail at proof planning; they exhibit unfaithful explanations that rationalize rather than justify their answers; they can be jailbroken completely using simple adaptive search. Each of these papers is highly cited because it answers a question that matters. None of them together resolve how to build reasoning systems that are both capable and robust, which may explain why the field continues producing both capability demonstrations and fragility measurements without convergence.

What does this collection reveal that the reading does not? First, the density of healthcare papers suggests this sector is where tension between claimed capability and actual deployment is sharpest and most costly. Second, the persistence of papers on hallucination, bias, unfaithful explanations, and jailbreaking indicates that alignment and safety improvements have not kept pace with scaling. Third, the absence of any papers addressing the computational or energy constraints behind these models means capability claims are being made in isolation from resource constraints that may be binding.

Does the data show whether models are improving on the fragility dimensions or just improving on benchmarks? No. The papers are chronologically sparse relative to the questions they raise, and many span the same model families or test periods. What they show instead is that benchmark improvement and robustness improvement are decoupled.

Is there a reason healthcare is so heavily represented? The data do not explain this, but the pattern is clear: healthcare has both high stakes for failure and measurable ground truth, making it possible to discover gaps between benchmark and reality that other sectors may not surface until deployment.

---

What does chain-of-thought prompting actually do to model reasoning?

It reframes reasoning as an inference-time technique rather than requiring retraining or fine-tuning. Models prompted to show intermediate steps improve sharply on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. The effect emerges around 100B parameters and is measurable without any weight updates. However, subsequent work shows this improvement is fragile: changing numbers in math problems degrades performance, adding irrelevant clauses cuts accuracy up to 65 percent, and models can rationalize biased answers without mentioning the biases that influenced them.

Why do models pass medical exams but fail on real patient cases?

Exam questions and real cases distribute differently. Med-PaLM reached 67.6 percent on USMLE-style questions. Hager et al. tested state-of-the-art models against 2,400 actual intensive-care cases and found they diagnosed worse than physicians, ignored treatment guidelines, and struggled to process lab results. The data do not explain why the distribution gap exists, but they confirm it is large and persistent.

Can safety alignment withstand simple attacks?

No. Andriushchenko et al. achieved 100 percent jailbreak success across all major frontier models using adaptive search to append optimized suffixes. The technique works because it targets each model's logit structure directly. The data show this applies to GPT-4o, Llama-3, Gemma, and Claude variants, but do not explain why these defenses remain vulnerable despite being explicitly trained for safety.

What happens to reasoning quality when models reason in hidden states instead of words?

The data do not cover this directly, but one paper notes that Coconut reasons in continuous latent space rather than generating visible reasoning steps, which removes the readable trace that auditors currently rely on. This complicates any audit framework that assumes explanations are faithful records of decision-making.

Do the papers show whether benchmark contamination explains performance gaps?
